query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored thermo‐mechanical processing protocol that combines severe cold rolling (~70% reduction) with a short duration high‐temperature annealing (600–700 °C for ∼1 hour) can refine the as-cast high-entropy alloy microstructure into an ultrafine duplex (lamellar) structure that simultaneously improves strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic or as‐cast high-entropy alloys (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1 or similar systems) exhibiting a coarse or composite lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply severe cold rolling (≈70% thickness reduction) to increase dislocation density followed by a controlled heat treatment (annealing at 600–700 °C for 1 hour) to promote recrystallization with phase refinement.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing performed at room temperature on specimens processed under strictly controlled rolling reduction and annealing parameters; the process must avoid excessive grain growth or unwanted phase decomposition. The method is expected to be most effective for HEAs predisposed to forming duplex microstructures and may not hold if the alloy composition or processing parameters do not favor fine-scale duplex formation.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine duplex microstructure with hierarchically distributed hard and soft phases (inherited lamellae refined by recrystallization), which promotes a two-hierarchical constraint effect and microcrack deflection or arrest.
generation.mechanism: The severe deformation induces high dislocation density and energy storage, which, when followed by rapid annealing, drives localized recrystallization and phase separation. The developed ultrafine duplex structure combines fine grain strengthening with phase interface hardening, leading to improvements in yield strength and ductility, and stabilizes fracture resistance and elastic modulus through heterogeneous phase distribution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally processed (e.g., solution-treated) alloys, this processing route is expected to yield samples with significantly higher yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (improvements potentially in the range of 25–40% or more) while maintaining or slightly enhancing ductility and fracture resistance as measured by appropriate standardized tests.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloys produced by conventional casting and standard heat treatment without the severe cold rolling step, which typically display coarser microstructures and less balanced mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The benefits may not be realized in HEA compositions that do not easily form duplex microstructures; further, over-processing (excessive rolling or annealing) could lead to grain coarsening or undesirable phase transformations that negate the improvements. Environmental or testing conditions (e.g., elevated temperatures or corrosive settings) may also alter the outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal balance between deformation severity and annealing conditions across different HEA chemistries. Additionally, while literature suggests a positive trend, the precise magnitude of improvement and potential trade-offs between ductility and strength require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical HEA samples. Process one set with the proposed thermo‐mechanical protocol (≈70% cold rolling followed by 1 h annealing at 600–700 °C) and another set using the baseline conventional processing. Subject both sets to standardized tensile, compression, and fracture toughness tests. Additionally, use microscopy (e.g., TEM/SEM) to characterize the microstructure refinement.
measurements: Grain size and phase distribution via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermo-mechanically processed samples do not show statistically significant improvements (≥25% increase in strength without loss of ductility and enhanced fracture resistance) over the baseline, or if the refined microstructure is not observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Tensile engineering stress–strain curves (Fig. 2a) show that although the solution-treated (ST) sample is soft (yield strength of ~274 MPa), remarkable strength increases occur in the samples after 72% cold rolling followed by ageing for 1 h at 600 °C and 700 °C (hereinafter named 600 A and 700 A, respectively). The maximum strengthening observed in 600 A is >1500 MPa (strength increment >560%), achieving ultrahigh yield strength (YS) of 1810 MPa and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 1905 MPa. Moreover, the YS and UTS of 700 A are 1570 MPa and 1763 MPa, respectively, which are ~1200 MPa (~430%) higher than those of the ST sample. In addition, both 600 A and 700 A exhibit good ductility (~9–10%) and excellent work-hardening capacity (uniform elongation to fracture). The exceptional combination of properties makes our alloy Al0.5Cr0.9FeNi2.5V0.2 superior to most traditional alloys for potential advanced structural applications.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs.
